document.title: Joint Protest of Calibrant Energy et al. to PJM Interconnection, LLC’s proposed revisions to its Open Access Transmission Tariff
document.filer: Calibrant EnergyAntora Energy LLCEolian, L.P. ,Convergent Energy and Power LP ,Mainspring Energy ,

pages.text:
1 
 
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
) 
PJM Interconnection, LLC 
) 
Docket No. ER26-1479-000 
) 
 
JOINT PROTEST OF BTMG PARTIES 
 
Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (Commission) 
Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 Calibrant Energy (Calibrant), Antora Energy, Inc. (Antora), 
Convergent Energy and Power (Convergent), Eolian L.P. (Eolian), and Mainspring Energy, Inc. 
(Mainspring) (together, BTMG Parties) respectfully submit this protest to PJM Interconnection, 
LLC’s (PJM) proposed revisions to its Open Access Transmission Tariff (Tariff) behind-the-
meter generation (BTMG) provisions in compliance with the Commission’s December 18, 2025 
order (Co-Location Order).2 BTMG Parties request that the Commission reject PJM’s filing and 
require further compliance to ensure that PJM’s revised Retail BTMG rules comply with the Co-
Location Order and are just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory or preferential. 
PJM’s proposed Retail BTMG definition must be rejected because it does not comply 
with the Commission’s directives in the Co-Location Order. Most significantly, PJM failed to 
file revisions that impose a “MW threshold for the amount of load that Network Customers may 
net by using BTMG” as directed in ordering paragraph (F) of the Co-Location Order.3 Rather 
 
1 18 C.F.R. § 385.211. 
2 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217, at PP 2, 161, 231-36 (2025) (Co-Location 
Order). 
3 Id. at Ordering P (F); see also id. P 179 (“we direct PJM to maintain the current BTMG rules 
for customers that fall below a new MW materiality threshold for the amount of load at a 
particular electrical location that Network Customers may net using BTMG.”); id. P 221 (“We 
therefore direct PJM, within 60 days of the date of issuance of this order, to propose a new MW 
threshold for the amount of load at a particular electrical location that Network Customers may 
net by using BTMG.”).

2 
 
than limit what load a Network Customer may net, PJM proposes a limit on the amount of 
nameplate generation that may qualify as a Retail BTMG. A threshold based on generation is 
plainly not a limit based on the load that is being netted. Such a nameplate generation-based 
threshold is also unjust and unreasonable and unduly discriminatory because it would also 
unnecessarily constrain commercial opportunities to serve loads with BTMG without better 
protecting reliability or commensurate reductions in resource adequacy or cost shift risks and 
treat differently BTMGs with similar resource adequacy and cost shift impacts. In the alternative, 
the Commission should require PJM to increase its proposed nameplate rating-based materiality 
threshold for Retail BTMG eligibility to 200 MW to preserve load opportunities to realize the 
commercial benefit of sizing nameplate generation above the amount of load that a retail 
customer seeks to net while still achieving the Commission’s aim of limiting resource adequacy 
impacts and cost shift concerns.  
PJM’s proposed grandfathering and transition period provisions also are not just and 
reasonable. PJM’s proposed use of the December 18, 2025 date of the Co-Location Order as the 
deadline for transition period and grandfathering eligibility threatens to needlessly exclude retail 
customers that recently finalized or will imminently finalize projects after months or years of 
development effort at a cost of millions of dollars while providing limited system benefit. This 
outcome would be particularly inequitable because the Co-Location Order provided notice to 
market participants that a materiality threshold based on the amount of load that a BTMG may 
net would be adopted. As a result, retail customers that finalized or will soon finalize 
arrangements in reliance on an expectation that a net load-based threshold would be adopted 
could be entirely excluded from netting eligibility. PJM should therefore be required to provide a 
modest additional period of time for the grandfathering and transition period by using the date of

3 
 
a Commission Order acting on PJM’s filing, or, at minimum, 180 days from the December 18, 
2025 date of the Co-Location Order (June 16, 2026),4 as the date from which the grandfathering 
and transition period run. The modest addition of several weeks to the eligibility deadline would  
better afford a workable transition for market participants that does not penalize developers for 
attempting to develop resources during a historic resource adequacy crisis in PJM.5  
I. 
BTMG PARTIES’ INTEREST IN THE PROCEEDING 
Calibrant develops energy generation and storage assets throughout the United States. 
Calibrant and its partners have developed and expect to continue to develop projects in PJM 
through a range of configurations, including BTMG and co-located projects supporting large 
loads. Specifically, Calibrant has several existing BTMG projects and projects that are currently 
being developed worth millions of dollars that will be impacted by PJM’s proposed revisions to 
its Retail BTMG rules.  
Antora is a U.S. manufacturer of thermal batteries, which are domestically built in San 
Jose, California, and developer of thermal storage projects for industrial facilities in the U.S. and 
abroad.  
Convergent develops, owns, and operates distributed energy storage and storage plus 
solar resources for large commercial, industrial, and utility customers across North American 
markets, including PJM. Convergent has resources in operation and in development in PJM, 
 
4 BTMG Developers suggest this date because it would allow the small number of customers 
actively finalizing deals to vindicate their investments and commercial expectations, but note 
that a shorter additional period would similarly be beneficial to vindicate the expectations of at 
least some of those customers. 
5 PJM 2027/2028 Base Residual Auction Report, at 3 (Dec. 17, 2025), https://www.pjm.com/-
/media/DotCom/markets-ops/rpm/rpm-auction-info/2027-2028/2027-2028-bra-report.pdf 
(explaining that the Base Residual Auction for the 2027/2028 Delivery Year cleared 6,516.6 
MW short of the reliability requirement).

4 
 
including behind-the-meter distribution and transmission connected battery energy storage 
systems, front-of-the-meter distribution connected battery energy storage systems, both with and 
without attached solar systems, and a 20 MW flywheel resource in Hazleton, Pennsylvania.  
Eolian develops energy generation and storage assets throughout the United States and 
has originated 27 GW of operating capacity to date. Eolian and its partners have developed 
projects supporting large loads in multiple regions across the United States, including PJM.  
Mainspring is a U.S.-headquartered manufacturer of modular, fuel-flexible, and 
dispatchable linear generators, a new type of power generator. Mainspring was founded in 2010 
and its first commercial units were deployed in 2020. The company has been rapidly scaling 
since 2023, deploying its innovative technology across a wide spectrum of customer types and 
use cases. The company’s customers include investor-owned utilities, public power utilities, 
municipal water treatment facilities, biogas facilities, data centers, grocery store chains, cold 
food storage, and hospital systems.  Mainspring’s linear generators can be installed behind a 
customer’s utility meter or as a front of the meter grid asset. Mainspring’s linear generators are 
currently operating across multiple sites in PJM territory and are in development across 
additional sites. 
BTMG Parties therefore have a substantial interest in this proceeding. Granting this 
limited protest will critically support development of BTMG resources while managing 
reliability and resource adequacy risks.6  
II. 
ARGUMENT 
A. 
The Commission must reject PJM’s BTMG materiality threshold because it 
does not comply with the Co-Location Order, is not just and reasonable, and is 
unduly discriminatory. 
 
 
6 Co-Location Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at PP 186, 221.

5 
 
1. 
PJM’s proposed materiality threshold does not comply with the 
Commission’s Co-Location Order. 
 
The Commission must reject PJM’s proposed BTMG materiality threshold because it 
does not comply with the Commission’s directive in the Co-Location Order. PJM failed to file 
revisions that impose a “MW threshold for the amount of load that Network Customers may net 
by using BTMG” as directed in ordering paragraph (F) of the Order.7 Rather than limit what load 
a Network Customer may net, PJM proposes a limit on the amount of nameplate generation that 
may qualify as BTMG.8 Generation is not load. A threshold based on generation capacity is 
plainly not a limit based on the load that is being netted. 
The Co-Location Order is not ambiguous on this point; the directive in the substantive 
portions of the order, including the rationale underlying the Commission’s Federal Power Act 
(FPA) Section 206 finding and the relevant ordering paragraph, each require action to limit the 
load that a customer may net.9 The Commission found PJM’s existing BTMG provision are not 
just and reasonable because they “do not limit the amount of qualifying load that a Network 
Customer may net by using BTMG and do not provide any protections against this potential 
transmission and resource adequacy planning problem or against the costs of maintaining 
sufficient resources to serve these loads being shifted onto other customers.”10 The Commission      
was motivated by the potential for large amounts of netting to occur through BTMG 
 
7 Id. at Ordering P (F); see also, id. P 221 (“We therefore direct PJM, within 60 days of the date 
of issuance of this order, to propose a new MW threshold for the amount of load at a particular 
electrical location that Network Customers may net by using BTMG.”). 
8 PJM Filing at 7 (“‘Retail Behind The Meter Generation’ shall refer to Behind The Meter 
Generation that is used to serve a retail load served by a Network Customer located at the same 
electrical location, where such generation has a cumulative nameplate rating of no greater than 
50 MW.”) 
9 Co-Location Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at PP 186, 221, (F). 
10 Id. P 186.

6 
 
arrangements, given that “PJM, per its Tariff, is obligated to serve transmission customers using 
BTMG but does not consider such customers in transmission and resource adequacy planning.”11 
The scale of the reduction in load (i.e., what PJM considers and plans for versus what PJM may 
actually need to serve) is the dispositive factor that determines whether the potential for resource 
adequacy problems and cost-shifts are problematic—not the nameplate of the generation used to 
effect the load reduction. 
2. 
Failure to reject PJM’s non-compliant proposal would violate notice 
requirements. 
 
PJM’s deviation from the Co-Location Order’s compliance directive is material. As 
discussed further below, a materiality threshold based on nameplate generation harms BTMG 
Parties, other developers of BTMG, and customers who seek to rely on BTMG by unjustly and 
unreasonably limiting the configurations that may qualify as BTMG. Parties were not on notice, 
given the clarity of the Co-Location Order’s directive to impose a limit on net loads, that the 
Commission’s determination could encompass a materiality threshold based on nameplate 
generation. 12 Parties such as the BTMG Parties therefore lacked an opportunity to request 
rehearing of a determination that harms their interests. Accepting PJM’s filing would violate 
BTMG Parties and other parties’ procedural rights to notice and to seek rehearing and to 
potentially appeal the Co-Location Order.13  
 
11 Id.  
12 Cf Southwest Power Pool, Inc., 182 FERC ¶ 61,100 at PP 34-35 (2023) (granting rehearing 
and reversing the Commission’s acceptance of proposed tariff provisions over concerns about 
“lack of adequate notice to interested parties” that “do[] not comport with the notice 
requirement” of the FPA and Commission regulations). 
13 To the extent that the Commission seeks to permit PJM to propose a materiality threshold 
other than one based on net loads, the procedurally proper means to achieve such an outcome 
would be for the Commission to grant rehearing, amend the directives in the Co-Location Order, 
and explain its reasoning to justify the new substantive outcome, which would allow aggrieved 
parties to then raise their concerns on rehearing. See 16 U.S.C. § 825l (a) (“the Commission may

7 
 
3. 
PJM’s proposal based on nameplate generation is not just and 
reasonable because it limits commercial opportunities for BTMG without 
providing additional commensurate system benefits. 
 
PJM’s materiality threshold based on nameplate generation unnecessarily constrains 
access to BTMG arrangements without providing commensurate system benefits and is 
therefore unjust and unreasonable. By focusing on nameplate generation, PJM’s proposal cuts 
off the potential for the routine, relatively small-scale upsizing of generation above the amount 
of load that is netted, taking off the table a number of valuable BTMG configurations without 
providing additional system benefits in terms of reducing the risk of resource adequacy or cost-
shifting concerns.  
The Commission recognized the value of BTMG netting in the Co-Location Order, citing 
prior precedent finding that netting “encourages load response during periods when generation 
of transmission are in short supply and prices are rising” and may contribute to charges for use 
of PJM’s transmission system that are consistent with the principle of cost causation.14 The 
Commission sought to address risks, however, associated with BTMG netting at a very large 
scale made possible by the proliferation of large loads such as data centers in PJM.15 As 
reflected in the Commission’s directive to PJM to implement a materiality threshold that is 
based on reductions in load, the resource adequacy and cost-shifting risks of BTMG depend 
upon the scale of the netting that is allowed. As the Commission explained, “not all loads using 
BTMG are large loads that create the reliability and resource adequacy risks described above.”16 
 
. . . upon reasonable notice . . . modify or set aside, in whole or in part, any finding or order 
made or issued by it . . .”) (emphasis added). 
14 Co-Location Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 7 (citing PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 107 FERC 
¶ 61,113, at PP 27-28 (2004)). 
15 Id. at P 186. 
16 Id. at P 221.

8 
 
The Commission thus found that the just and reasonable replacement rate should strike a 
balance by limiting large scale BTMG netting while enabling smaller scale netting that does not 
contribute to reliability and resource adequacy risks in the same way. 
PJM’s proposed materiality threshold upsets that balance by limiting the availability of 
BTMG arrangements for loads even at the smaller scale. As seasoned developers of BTMG in 
PJM, BTMG Parties are aware of several common BTMG arrangements that would net no more 
than 50 MW of load, and therefore not raise the kinds of reliability, resource adequacy, or cost-
shifting risks of concern, but that would rely on more than 50 MW of nameplate generation. For 
example, it is not uncommon for BTMG configurations to rely on combinations of resources 
that have different availability profiles, such as solar and storage, to firm up the generation. In 
such arrangements, the combined nameplate generation is greater than the load reduction sought 
to be achieved in order to ensure that reduction can be achieved during the required hours of 
load operation. It is also common for nameplate BTMG to be somewhat oversized for loads that 
have the most stringent commercial expectations of reliable operation (the so-called “five nines” 
of reliable operation), as is the case for certain data centers. Such oversizing of the BTMG may 
be commercially valuable because it ensures the load can continue to be served by BTMG 
during partial outages, like when a unit may need to be taken offline to perform planned or 
unplanned maintenance. Or, in another routine case, customers may choose to upsize the scale 
of a battery storage system to address battery degradation that occurs over time, and to ensure 
that there is no disruption in operation of the load while replacement of that capacity occurs.        
Under each of these scenarios, the load netted would remain below the 50 MW threshold 
and therefore fall within the scope of the small scale BTMG netting that Commission found 
should be permitted under the Co-Location Order. Yet PJM’s proposal would prevent such

9 
 
beneficial arrangements from qualifying as BTMG, creating a barrier to this kind of 
arrangement without providing commensurate system benefits to justify the limitation.  
4. 
PJM’s proposal is also unduly discriminatory because it treats 
similarly situated load configurations differently. 
 
Using a nameplate-based materiality threshold rather than one based on the amount of 
load that can be netted treats behind the meter generators with similar impacts on resource 
adequacy and cost shifting differently and is therefore unduly discriminatory. As discussed 
above, the relevant characteristic of customers relying on BTMG is the scale of the reduction in 
load that they seek to achieve, because large scale reductions may result in resource adequacy 
and cost-shifting concerns. But PJM’s proposal treats BTMG configurations that achieve the 
same netting of load differently. For example, 30 MW of BTMG combined heat and power 
generation at one site and a hybrid 30 MW gas turbine plus 30 MW battery storage system at a 
different site, serving a different retail customer, can each be designed and operated to have the 
same impact on the grid, where each achieves no greater than a 30 MW reduction in the 
respective retail customer’s load, but the customer with the 30 MW BTMG diesel generation 
would be eligible for netting under PJM’s rules while the customer with a 60 MW combined 
nameplate hybrid system would not. This is particularly objectionable given that PJM’s Effective 
Load Carrying Capability (ELCC) recognizes the different resource adequacy profiles that 
different resources have and requires real-world addition to meet resource adequacy needs,17 
while PJM’s proposed BTMG rules would bind loads to nameplate metrics that do not reflect 
how these resources perform in the real world. 
 
17 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 191 FERC ¶ 61,203, at P 3 (2025).

10 
 
Additionally, PJM’s proposal would needlessly expose retail loads served by BTMG just 
above the materiality threshold to starkly different treatment than retail loads served by BTMG at 
or just below the threshold despite similar impacts on the grid. Under PJM’s proposed nameplate 
threshold, a 50 MW BTMG is eligible for netting but a 50.1 MW BTMG, which has near 
indistinguishable grid impacts, is fully ineligible to net. Under a threshold allowing 50 MW of 
netting, on the other hand, a BTMG that could avoid 50 MW of load would be eligible to net 50 
MW while one that could avoid 50.1 MW of net load would also be eligible to net 50 MW. 
While BTMG Parties recognize the need for line drawing in establishing market rules, a 
threshold based on net load would protect against the reliability and cost shift impacts that the 
Commission sought to address while providing for more continuous treatment to BTMGs on 
either side of the threshold line. 
5. 
A materiality threshold based on the amount customers may net is 
readily implementable and the Commission should require PJM to adopt it 
upon further compliance. 
 
PJM does not justify its failure to propose a materiality threshold based on net load other 
than to argue without supporting factual evidence that because “load sizes can fluctuate” and 
the nameplate rating of a generator “is static,” its proposal provides a clear and bright line.18 
But a threshold based on the amount that customer can net is readily implementable. Existing 
BTMG is already subject to metering and reporting requirements under PJM Manual 14D.19 
Under those requirements, or as a condition of BTMG interconnection agreements, and/or the 
 
18 PJM Filing at 14 (arguing therefore that its proposal is “consistent with or superior to” that the 
netting approach required by the Co-Location Order). 
19 PJM, Manual 14D: Generator Operational Requirements, Revision: 70, at 179 (Dec. 17, 
2025), https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/documents/manuals/m14d.pdf/ (“BTMG that is 
10 MW or greater (or has been identified as requiring metering for operational security reasons) 
must have both revenue metering and telemetering for operational security purposes.”).

11 
 
retail customer’s Electric Service Agreement with the Electric Distribution Utility, BTMG 
larger than 10 MW typically have installed sophisticated telemetry to ensure that exports and 
withdrawals from the grid remain within the required limits of the BTMG arrangement. BTMG 
Parties believe, based on its experience as BTMG developers in PJM, that the additional steps 
that may be necessary to monitor, control, and report on the amount of load being reduced by 
BTMG are technologically feasible, commercially viable, and readily implementable.20 Indeed, 
BTMG Parties’ battery electric storage systems are sub-metered, and their output can be 
controlled with sub-two-second precision. Because BTMG Parties’ BTMG resources often 
already participate in PJM’s most operationally rigorous markets, including Regulation, the 
resources must already be capable of precise signal-following and sub-metering at the battery 
system. If BTMG resources are capable of meeting the stringent telemetry and control 
requirements necessary for Regulation participation, the same metering and control capabilities 
can clearly support netting for the purposes of the materiality threshold.21 In sum, the metering, 
 
20 Elsewhere in its filing, PJM points to the challenges of so-called hybrid approaches, stating 
that allowing for such an approach would “impose significant costs” if BTMG had “to install 
previously unnecessary metering equipment (that, for some facilities, may be cost prohibitive)” 
and “amplifies compliance risks for units because it might require many facilities to monitor and 
report different generator output and load thresholds in relation to the threshold.” Id. at 11. It is 
not clear if PJM intends these statements to apply to BTMG in general, or just to hybrid 
approaches. In any event, PJM does not provide any factual support for these assertions, and 
these statements do not match BTMG Parties’ experience as developers of BTMG in PJM. To 
the contrary, BTMG arrangements larger than 10 MW typically already have experience with 
such metering equipment, monitoring and reporting obligations, and would not find such 
requirements cost prohibitive. 
21 Further, to ensure compliance with both non-export requirements (under the BTMG 
interconnection agreement) and maximum power draw limits (under the ESA contract capacity), 
while accounting in real time for the behavior of on-site load and other generation, BTMG 
Parties’ systems employ two additional safeguards: Minimum Import Power and Maximum 
Import Power controls. These controls establish operating margins around both net-zero export 
and the customer’s contracted capacity, ensuring that system operations remain fully compliant 
with all applicable obligations at all times. In short, because BTMG resources must have these

12 
 
telemetry, and control capabilities already deployed for existing BTMG resources demonstrate 
that BTMG can reliably comply with the operational requirements necessary to implement a 
netting-based threshold.  
Finally, to the extent that PJM lacks experience with monitoring and reporting on BTMG 
in its footprint, any current lack of transparency surrounding BTMG arrangements is not a 
basis for failing to adopt an approach that will develop these institutional capabilities and 
transparency today. Improved transparency and consistent reporting by both BTMG operators 
and LSEs would provide PJM with a clearer understanding of existing deployment levels and 
should alleviate concerns associated with implementing limits on BTMG netting. 
Accordingly, FERC should reject PJM’s proposed materiality threshold and require PJM 
to adopt a materiality threshold that allows BTMGs to net up to 50 MW of load.  
B. 
If the Commission accepts PJM’s non-compliant nameplate capacity-based 
threshold for Retail BTMG eligibility, it should at least require PJM to adopt the 
200 MW threshold to limit potential harm. 
 
PJM asks, if the Commission does not accept PJM’s proposed Retail BTMG revisions, 
for the Commission to “allow an interim materiality threshold to be in place for the start of the 
transition period,” potentially to be further refined in later filings.22 As to the potential level of 
this interim threshold, PJM “observes that the PJM Industrial Customer Coalition . . . indicated 
that ‘a threshold of 200 MW would, as a practical matter, permit most existing industrial and 
institutional loads to continue to benefit from the major energy investments they have made over 
decades . . . .’”23 Moreover, PJM’s willingness to accept a 200 MW nameplate generation 
 
capabilities for other requirements, a threshold based on netting is technologically and 
commercially feasible. 
22 PJM Filing at 14-15. 
23 Id. at 15.

13 
 
materiality threshold while it gathers more information on the need for a more stringent threshold 
is a strong indication that PJM believes such a threshold would be sufficient to address concerns 
about reliability, resource adequacy, and cost-shifting. 
BTMG Parties maintain that the Commission should require PJM to comply with the 
plain language of the Co-Location Order, as discussed above. If the Commission is inclined to 
accept PJM’s nameplate capacity-based threshold,24 however, it should require PJM to adopt the 
alternative 200 MW threshold identified in PJM’s filing rather than PJM’s proposed 50 MW 
threshold. This higher MW threshold would more appropriately preserve load opportunities 
(such as the examples provided above) to realize the commercial benefit of sizing nameplate 
generation above the amount of load that a retail customer seeks to net while still achieving the 
Commission’s aim of limiting resource adequacy impacts and cost shift concerns.  
C. 
The Commission must reject PJM’s BTMG grandfathering provisions 
because the proposed transition period and grandfathering deadlines are unjust and 
unreasonable to existing BTMG customers. 
 
BTMG Parties also request that the Commission reject the deadlines that PJM proposes 
for BTMG resources to qualify for PJM’s grandfathering and transition provisions. 
Notwithstanding PJM’s proposed 50 MW nameplate BTMG eligibility threshold, PJM proposes 
to grandfather BTMGs that were in certain arrangements as of December 18, 2025, i.e., the date 
that the Commission issued the Co-Location Order.25 Specifically, PJM proposes to provide a 
three year transition period of continued eligibility for BTMGs larger than 50 MW serving retail 
loads prior to December 18, 2025, and to grandfather eligibility for BTMGs used to serve retail 
 
24 To the extent that the Commission permits PJM to retain a nameplate capacity-based 
threshold, BTMG Parties understand that nameplate capacity will be based on the amount 
contemplated in relevant interconnection agreements or similar documents. 
25 Id. at 8-11.

14 
 
load subject to contractual arrangements or as Qualifying Facilities under the Public Utility 
Regulatory Policies Act of 1978 as of December 18, 2025.26 These deadlines threatens to deny 
many customers that have been diligently developing BTMG resources over the past several 
years the ability to benefit from millions in investments that could otherwise help to mitigate the 
historic reliability crisis in PJM.27 Moreover, it imposes this harsh outcome during a time when 
PJM’s interconnection queue pause28 and uncertainty over the rules for co-located arrangements 
left BTMG the main remaining viable path for new resources. Instead, the Commission should 
reject PJM’s proposed transition period and grandfathering deadlines and direct PJM to adopt a 
modest additional period of time29 to allow grandfathering and transition period eligibility for 
BTMGs that were in specified arrangements as of the date of the Commission’s order on PJM’s 
compliance filing, or, in the alternative, 180 days from the December 18, 2025 date of the Co-
Location Order (i.e., June 16, 2026). 30 
 
26 Id. 
27 PJM 2027/2028 Base Residual Auction Report, at 3 (Dec. 17, 2025), https://www.pjm.com/-
/media/DotCom/markets-ops/rpm/rpm-auction-info/2027-2028/2027-2028-bra-report.pdf 
(explaining that the Base Residual Auction for the 2027/2028 Delivery Year cleared 6,516.6 
MW short of the reliability requirement). 
28 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 181 FERC ¶ 61,162, at P 60 (2022).  
29 The Commission has authority to direct such an extension because the Co-Location Order did 
not specify the date from which the grandfathering period should run. 
30 The Commission has found filings with inadequate transition periods unjust and unreasonable 
and directed filing of revised provisions including longer transitions. See Midwest Indep. 
Transmission Sys. Operator, Inc., 138 FERC ¶ 61,233, at P 104 (2012) (finding unjust and 
unreasonable a proposal requiring projects with outstanding interconnection requests to transition 
to proposed revised generator interconnection procedures one day after issuance of the order 
accepting them and directing submission of revisions allowing a 90 day transition from the date 
of an order accepting the revised generator interconnection procedures). The Commission has 
also “rejected revisions where it found settled expectations outweighed any benefits or where it 
found proposed revisions resulted in no benefit at all or were even discriminatory.” ISO New 
England Inc. & New England Power Pool, 145 FERC ¶ 61,095, at P 29 (2013); ISO New 
England Inc., 134 FERC ¶ 61,128, at PP 39-40 (2011); see also Cap. Power Corp. v. FERC, 156 
F.4th 644, 651–52 (D.C. Cir. 2025) (“FERC failed to adequately explain why these reliance 
interests were either inconsequential or outweighed by countervailing considerations . . . FERC

15 
 
Accepting PJM’s proposed grandfathering and transition period deadlines could leave 
retail customers who have been developing projects for several years and have invested millions 
in infrastructure to serve loads wholly ineligible to net, upsetting commercial expectations and 
threatening project viability. Conversely, requiring a modest additional time period prior to 
commencement of the grandfathering and transition eligibility deadlines would avoid significant 
harm to those customers while maintaining firm deadlines for PJM’s new Retail BTMG 
paradigm going forward, as the Co-Location Order contemplates. In addition, extending the 
grandfathering and transition period deadlines will not impose material reliability or resource 
adequacy costs onto the system or other customers because only the limited class of BTMG 
developers that were very close to finalizing their projects will be able to benefit from it—i.e., 
those that have the greatest investments at risk should PJM’s proposed deadlines stand. This 
class is limited because the lead times required to develop generation infrastructure far exceed 
the time contemplated in the modest extension requested here, especially given supply chain 
constraints and siting challenges. The limited addition of time to the grandfathering and 
transition eligibility deadlines would therefore provide critical benefits to resources that have 
worked diligently in recent months to pair development of retail loads with new supply while 
imposing minimal adverse impacts on others.  
A modest extension to the deadlines for the purpose of the transition period or 
grandfathering eligibility is all the more necessary given the degree to which PJM’s filing 
 
never considered a more gradual elimination of reactive-power compensation . . . Nor did FERC 
explain why immediate elimination is reasonable despite the generators’ long-term power 
obligations and accompanying investments. Put differently, although compensation cannot be 
guaranteed forever, that does not suggest it could reasonably be eliminated overnight.”). Here, 
the requested additional time prior to commencement of the grandfathering and transition period 
deadline is required to mitigate disruption of settled expectations and therefore to ensure that the 
benefits of the proposed revisions outweigh their impact to settled expectations.

16 
 
deviates from the Co-Location Order’s requirements in proposing a nameplate capacity-based 
materiality threshold, as discussed above. The Co-Location Order did not provide retail 
customers effective notice that PJM could adopt a nameplate capacity-based threshold, which, as 
discussed, could leave them wholly ineligible to net any load if they exceed the 50 MW cutoff. 
As a result, BTMGs that effectuated contractual arrangements after issuance of the Co-Location 
Order based on the expectation that any limits would be based on the BTMG’s net effects on the 
system could be left entirely ineligible to net either under the new Retail BTMG definition or the 
grandfathering provisions. Such a restriction would unreasonably upset these entities’ settled 
expectations.  
The December 18, 2025 deadlines for the transition period and grandfathering are 
therefore unjust and unreasonable. Accordingly, and in particular because the Co-Location Order 
did not provide actual notice of the form of PJM’s proposed BTMG materiality threshold, the 
Commission should reject PJM’s proposed December 18, 2025 deadlines for grandfathering and 
the transition period and instead direct PJM to set the date of the Commission’s order on PJM’s 
compliance filing as the deadlines for such eligibility.  
III. 
CONCLUSION 
BTMG Parties respectfully request that the Commission reject PJM’s compliance filing 
and direct PJM to file revisions that (1) impose a materiality threshold for qualifying as BTMG 
based on the amount of load a customer may net, or, in the alternative, increase the nameplate 
threshold to the 200 MW referenced in PJM’s filing; and (2) set the deadlines for grandfathering 
and transition period eligibility as the date of the Commission’s order in this proceeding.  
 
 
Respectfully submitted,
